questions.q: A filling of the Young diagram of shape $\lambda = (2,2)$ is a semistandard Young tableau (SSYT) exactly when:
choices: rows strictly increase left to right and columns strictly increase top to bottom
rows weakly increase left to right and columns strictly increase top to bottom
rows weakly increase and columns weakly increase
every entry from $1$ to $n$ appears exactly once
questions.explain: An SSYT is row-weak and column-strict: entries weakly increase along each row (repeats allowed) and strictly increase down each column. The all-distinct $1\ldots n$ condition with strict rows is instead the definition of a standard Young tableau (SYT).

questions.q: Let $\lambda = (3,1)$ with conjugate $\lambda' = (2,1,1)$. Which statements are true?
choices: $\lambda$ is a partition of $n = 4$
The Young diagram of $\lambda$ has $4$ cells
Conjugation reflects the diagram across its main diagonal, swapping rows and columns
$\lambda$ and $\lambda'$ always have the same number of parts
questions.explain: $\lambda=(3,1)$ has $|\lambda| = 3+1 = 4$, so it partitions $4$ and its diagram has $4$ cells. The conjugate $\lambda'$ is the transpose: its $j$-th part counts cells in column $j$, i.e. the diagram reflected across the main diagonal. The number of parts of $\lambda'$ equals $\lambda_1$ (the longest row), not the number of parts of $\lambda$ in general — here $\lambda$ has $2$ parts but $\lambda'=(2,1,1)$ has $3$.

questions.q: Is the filling $\begin{smallmatrix}1 & 1 & 2\\ 2 & 3\end{smallmatrix}$ of shape $(3,2)$ a valid semistandard Young tableau (entries from $\{1,2,3\}$)?
choices: Yes: rows weakly increase and columns strictly increase
No: the first row $1,1,2$ is not strictly increasing
No: column $1$ has $1$ then $2$, which is not allowed
No: the entry $3$ may not appear in a $3$-cell row
questions.explain: Row $1$ is $1,1,2$ (weakly increasing, repeats allowed — fine for SSYT) and row $2$ is $2,3$. Column $1$ is $1 < 2$ and column $2$ is $1 < 3$, both strictly increasing. So it is a valid SSYT. (It would not be standard, since entries repeat and are not the distinct values $1\ldots5$.)

questions.q: For $\lambda = (2,2)$ the cell hook lengths are $3, 2, 2, 1$. The hook length formula gives the number of standard Young tableaux as $f^\lambda = n! / \prod \text{hook}(c)$. Compute $f^{(2,2)}$.
questions.explain: Here $n = 4$, so $f^{(2,2)} = 4! / (3\cdot 2\cdot 2\cdot 1) = 24/12 = 2$. The two standard tableaux fill $(2,2)$ as $\begin{smallmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{smallmatrix}$ and $\begin{smallmatrix}1&3\\2&4\end{smallmatrix}$.

questions.q: For $\lambda = (3,1)$ the hook lengths are $4, 2, 1, 1$. How many standard Young tableaux does it have?
questions.explain: $n = 4$ and $\prod \text{hook} = 4\cdot 2\cdot 1\cdot 1 = 8$, so $f^{(3,1)} = 24/8 = 3$. (The corner cell of the first row has hook $4 = $ arm $2$ + leg $1$ + the cell itself.)

questions.q: The hook length of a cell $c$ in a Young diagram is defined as:
choices: the number of cells directly below $c$
the number of cells in the same row plus the same column
$\text{arm}(c) + \text{leg}(c) + 1$: cells strictly to the right, plus cells strictly below, plus $c$ itself
the row index plus the column index of $c$
questions.explain: The hook of $c$ consists of $c$, the cells to its right in the same row (the arm), and the cells below it in the same column (the leg). So $\text{hook}(c) = \text{arm}(c) + \text{leg}(c) + 1$. The product of all hook lengths divides $n!$ to give $f^\lambda$.

questions.q: Which of the following are bases of the ring $\Lambda$ of symmetric functions, each indexed by partitions?
choices: the monomial symmetric functions $m_\lambda$
the elementary symmetric functions $e_\lambda$
the complete homogeneous symmetric functions $h_\lambda$
the power-sum symmetric functions $p_\lambda$
questions.explain: All four families $\{m_\lambda\}, \{e_\lambda\}, \{h_\lambda\}, \{p_\lambda\}$ are bases of $\Lambda$ (the power sums require coefficients in $\mathbb{Q}$, but still span). The Schur functions $s_\lambda$ are a fifth, distinguished basis.

questions.q: In two variables $x_1, x_2$, the elementary symmetric function $e_2$ and the complete homogeneous $h_2$ are:
questions.explain: $e_2$ sums over strictly increasing index pairs: $e_2 = x_1 x_2$. The complete $h_2$ sums all degree-$2$ monomials: $h_2 = x_1^2 + x_1 x_2 + x_2^2$. In general $e_k$ uses distinct factors while $h_k$ allows repeats.

questions.q: Newton's identities relate the power sums $p_k$ to the elementary symmetric functions. The first one reads:
questions.explain: Both $p_1 = \sum_i x_i$ and $e_1 = \sum_i x_i$ are the sum of the variables, so $p_1 = e_1$. The next identity is $p_2 = e_1 p_1 - 2 e_2$; Newton's identities recursively express every $p_k$ in the $e$'s (and vice versa).

questions.q: The Schur function $s_\lambda$ is defined combinatorially as:
choices: $\sum_T x^{\text{content}(T)}$ summed over all semistandard Young tableaux $T$ of shape $\lambda$
the product of the hook lengths of $\lambda$
$\sum_T x^{\text{content}(T)}$ summed over all standard tableaux of shape $\lambda$
the number of partitions of $|\lambda|$
questions.explain: $s_\lambda = \sum_T x^{\text{content}(T)}$ over SSYT $T$ of shape $\lambda$, where $\text{content}(T)$ records how many times each value appears. The coefficient of the monomial $x^\mu$ is the Kostka number $K_{\lambda\mu}$, the number of SSYT of shape $\lambda$ and content $\mu$.

questions.q: How many semistandard Young tableaux of shape $\lambda = (2,1)$ have entries drawn from $\{1,2,3\}$? (Equivalently, $s_{(2,1)}(1,1,1)$ — the total number of monomials counted with multiplicity in $s_{(2,1)}(x_1,x_2,x_3)$.)
questions.explain: There are $8$ such SSYT. As monomials, $s_{(2,1)}(x_1,x_2,x_3) = x_1^2 x_2 + x_1^2 x_3 + x_1 x_2^2 + x_1 x_3^2 + x_2^2 x_3 + x_2 x_3^2 + 2\,x_1 x_2 x_3$. The coefficient $2$ on $x_1 x_2 x_3$ is the Kostka number $K_{(2,1),(1,1,1)} = 2$, and the total count is $6 + 2 = 8$.

questions.q: The Jacobi-Trudi formula expresses a Schur function as a determinant. For $\lambda = (2,1)$ it gives:
choices: $s_{(2,1)} = \det\begin{pmatrix} h_2 & h_3\\ h_0 & h_1\end{pmatrix} = h_2 h_1 - h_3$
$s_{(2,1)} = \det\begin{pmatrix} h_1 & h_2\\ h_0 & h_1\end{pmatrix}$
questions.explain: Jacobi-Trudi: $s_\lambda = \det(h_{\lambda_i - i + j})$. For $\lambda = (2,1)$ the $2\times 2$ matrix has entries $h_{\lambda_i - i + j}$, giving $\begin{pmatrix}h_2 & h_3\\ h_0 & h_1\end{pmatrix}$ and $s_{(2,1)} = h_2 h_1 - h_3$ (using $h_0 = 1$). Checking at $x_1=x_2=x_3=1$: $h_1=3, h_2=6, h_3=10$, so $6\cdot 3 - 10 = 8$, matching the SSYT count.

questions.q: The Robinson-Schensted-Knuth correspondence is a bijection between permutations of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ and:
choices: pairs $(P, Q)$ of standard Young tableaux of the same shape $\lambda \vdash n$
single standard tableaux with $n$ cells
partitions of $n$
pairs of standard tableaux of arbitrary (possibly different) shapes
questions.explain: RSK bijects each permutation with an ordered pair $(P, Q)$ of standard Young tableaux of the same shape $\lambda \vdash n$ ($P$ is the insertion tableau, $Q$ the recording tableau). Counting both sides gives $\sum_{\lambda \vdash n} (f^\lambda)^2 = n!$.

questions.q: Summing over all partitions $\lambda$ of $n$, the RSK bijection proves $\sum_{\lambda \vdash n} (f^\lambda)^2 = \,?$, where $f^\lambda$ is the number of standard Young tableaux of shape $\lambda$. Enter the value for $n = 4$.
Applying Schensted row insertion (RSK) to the permutation $3\,1\,4\,2$ yields a pair $(P, Q)$. What is the common shape of $P$ and $Q$?
questions.explain: Row-inserting $3,1,4,2$ in turn: $3$; then $1$ bumps $3$ to a new row; then $4$ joins the first row; then $2$ bumps $4$ down. The insertion tableau is $P = \begin{smallmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{smallmatrix}$ with recording $Q = \begin{smallmatrix}1&3\\2&4\end{smallmatrix}$, both of shape $(2,2)$. The first row length $2$ equals the longest increasing subsequence (e.g. $3,4$ or $1,2$).

questions.q: The irreducible representations of the symmetric group $S_n$ over $\mathbb{C}$ are indexed by:
choices: partitions $\lambda \vdash n$, with $\dim = f^\lambda$ the number of standard Young tableaux of shape $\lambda$
the integers $1, 2, \ldots, n$
conjugacy classes only, with no dimension formula
permutations of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$
questions.explain: The irreducible $S_n$-modules (Specht modules) are indexed by partitions $\lambda \vdash n$, and $\dim S^\lambda = f^\lambda$, the number of standard Young tableaux of shape $\lambda$. Summing $\sum_\lambda (\dim)^2 = \sum_\lambda (f^\lambda)^2 = n! = |S_n|$ recovers the general class-equation identity.

questions.q: Using $\dim S^\lambda = f^\lambda$ and $\lambda = (2,1) \vdash 3$ (hook lengths $3,1,1$), what is the dimension of the corresponding irreducible representation of $S_3$?
questions.explain: $f^{(2,1)} = 3! / (3\cdot 1\cdot 1) = 6/3 = 2$. This is the $2$-dimensional standard representation of $S_3$. The three irreducibles of $S_3$ have dimensions $1$ (trivial, $\lambda=(3)$), $2$ (standard, $\lambda=(2,1)$), and $1$ (sign, $\lambda=(1,1,1)$), with $1^2 + 2^2 + 1^2 = 6 = 3!$.
